questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: the academic quality of NUS as the leading university in Asia and in the global top, alongside  the deeply international setting in which NUS operates (both regarding Singapore as a global hub and the make-up of the institution itself), is what drew me to choosing my study destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy; given how overwhelming it is to suddenly find yourself in a new setting as an exchange student, it was still manageable to figure out which steps needed to be taken. NUS was prompt and quick to issue out thorough step-by-step guides and other informational e-mails prior to arrival in the host country.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Everything was pretty much pre-arranged by us students ourselves before arrival, as a lot of the orientation to life at NUS was done online prior to school start or needed you to book a timeslot (i.e. their initial course 'Consent and Respect Culture' with accompanying workshop).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: not really applicable, as 90% happened online before arrival. But they were quick to respond to questions etc. by mail.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Found it through Airbnb - so as any of their services, it was "easy" (the obvious price and budget considerations aside).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The NUS Campus (besides the faculty of law) is pretty far away from the city centre (45min-1h), so I found it more rewarding to live off campus in terms of getting to know the city and all the nooks and special places that can get overlooked when you're just visiting a big city and not having to actually figure out a life in it. However, living off campus also entails that you don't get the same sense of community with the other exchange students and locals which comes from living in the dormitories and being on campus all the time. Therefore, I'd say it's a give-and-take living on or off campus. I enjoyed having 'the experience of an NUS student' combined with the 'small human-big city'-kind of experience you get living on your own in a huge and unknown city, wherein you have to explore and establish your own sense of belonging and comfort in a place unfamiliar to you.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: very expensive living off campus - but that is given in the world's most expensive city

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: pretty confusing to be fair. As it is your own responsibility to make out a schedule with no overlapping subjects and not having a collective website to plan, it was hard navigating multiple websites and pages in order to check time tables, credit points, curriculum, availability etc.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The registration at NUS was two-tiered, as it required a part one and part two, simultaneously coinciding with the authorities' requirement of a Student Pass.

The first part you had to start your registration online, including uploading a photo, paying the miscellaneous administrative and health security fees, and accepting your offer. From there, the actual course registration commenced, which entailed you registrering to eligible courses. The second part of registration happened after arrival, and consisted of collection and activation of our student card.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I found that I could both use e-mail and telephone to their Registrar's office or academic activities office if I had any questions.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: not very succesful. At first I was unable to secure the credits I needed and I thus had to apply for courses again - but now from a significantly narrowed down selection.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: set out time and really invest in getting into the registration process, as all the steps required make it very overwhelming and time-consuming. It is not difficult, but just requires time.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses were of very high quality. The teachers were deeply ingrained in the subject matter, having dedicated their life to their specific field of law - which made for very inspiring and knowledgeable teaching. Furthermore, the style of teaching which included, i.a., that class participation was a part of the students' assessment, entailed a very engaging classroom; prompting for lengthy debates or elaborations in class.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was fundamentally different. At NUS, class attendance, class participation, mid-terms and other assignments all form part of your final assessment alongside the actual exam. This meant that you were constantly being evaluated academically by your professor and that preparation and school work took on a whole different meaning than at UCPH. At UCPH it is more geared towards the students' own independence and sense of responsibility regarding their approach to studying, whereas NUS did not follow the same idea of "with freedom comes responsibility."

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Multinational Enterprises and International Law
International Environmental Law
Law and the Humanities
Digital Technologies and Human Rights
Maritime Law

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All courses at NUS have a pretty broad international focus, which I liked, but out of the courses I chose I would probably recommend 'Multinational Enterprises and International Law,' as it showcased the actual approach by corporations and enterprises working in a global setting and how they function in cross-border instances - where different rules, jurisdictions and legal thinking operates. It really showed how you utilize and work with law in international settings, in "the real world."

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: none I can recall

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I think coming from Denmark is always an advantage when it comes to the prices of food and beverages, as our average prices of such things are quite high compared to the rest of the world - this means we can't really be shocked by the prices abroad. Therefore, I actually found food were less expensive than expected - generally, the concept of a hawker centre makes it possible to live rather cheap in Singapore. Other than those places, food and drink (both in restaurants and grocery and convenience stores) were priced like in Denmark / Copenhagen and above.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: as people live on campus, and campus is a city in and of itself, a wide array of activities were available. both regular things, like various sports clubs, and pop-ups, like open-air cinema, were planned by the school and its associations (open for registration for all).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: the pop-ups were always quite inventive - like they did an open-air cinema in the botanical gardens and a tour of the old districts of Singapore. I also think a sports club would be a great way to socialize with the locals, but I don't play any sport so I didn't do it myself.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Singapore is at the center of SE Asia, which means that you can, relatively easy and affordable, travel to the neighboring countries. Other than that, Singapore actually have a lot to offer in itself - from the more touristy activities like go-kart, boulders, cinema, amusement parks etc., located in downtown and Sentosa, to actual jungles and local nature where you can hike - MacRitchie Reservoir for example!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy. Singapore is a multicultural country and with strong international traction - which means that the city caters to everybody.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I found the local students to be very hardworking and use a lot of their time on their studies (as is expected with Singaporean work culture). However, they were open and very friendly, which made talking very easy - Singaporeans have a global mindset and are used to expats and exchange students, which means that they are also interested in hearing about you, and where you are coming from.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Singapore is very fast-paced, and in the beginning I found it overwhelming that everything is quite transactional and straight-to-business when you're out and about. Especially coming from Copenhagen/Denmark, where we're used to acknowledging each other with eye contact etc. as a form of polite gesture. But I think that their notion of respect might be different from ours, whereas in Singapore it is more of a respectful distance to each other and their time, than in Denmark.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: that the deeply multicultural setting made it possible to experience so many different people and their cultures, which is totally different from homogenous Denmark.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Prepare to study hard, as it is one of Asia's leading universities for a reason.
2. In a place where so many cultures and their distinct foods/activities/goods are within arm's length, remember to step out of your comfort zone and try them!
3. It is very safe and clean to walk around in Singapore - but for a reason. There are a lot of rules that we're not used to in Denmark.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: To enjoy the stay and that everyone has a different experience of going on exchange; comparing your stay to others makes no sense as this is about you and your own development - personally and academically.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I really felt that exchange provided a chance to self-reflect on a lot of things that one forget or put on autopilot when in your usual settings. It reminded me of the love of learning that drove me to university (which can kind of disappear in the everyday schoollife and grade anxiety), and I consider my exchange stay a huge gift and privilege. To be able to experience so much and also the many different impressions you get along the way really left an impact, as you learn to see your own life (back home) and what you want to keep or change - as the chance of crafting a new, temporary life on exchange enable you to form a comparative basis for assessing your own existence.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I think the greatest challenge was probably also the most rewarding part of the exchange: having to stand on your own two feet in a foreign country, having to ultimately take into your own hands the responsibility of shaping how your exchange semester is gonna look like, is really overwhelming and frightening. But in the end, it is also the most rewarding - as you successfully did it on your own.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: No.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
